clarifyingQuestions: Should file metadata affect the hash or only content and path?
Should deleting a directory delete all descendants?
Should rename detection be part of this structure or a separate diff layer?
followUps: Add ignore rules for `.git`, generated files, and vendor directories.
Hash large files from a stream of chunks.
Persist subtree hashes so changed files invalidate only ancestors.
followUpGuide: For ignore rules, normalize the path first, then check every prefix against exact directory rules and glob rules.
For streaming files, compute the file content hash from chunks, then update the tree with the final digest. Keep the tree API separate from the file reader.
For persistence, store each node by path with its kind, child names, and hash. A file update only needs to rewrite that file and its ancestor directories.
complexityAnalysis: - Let P be path characters, B content bytes, d path depth, c_i child count at ancestor i, and N_i the serialized child-name characters there. `set_file` time: O(P + B + sum(c_i log c_i + N_i)) with bounded-size digests. Extra space: O(P + B + d + max(c_i + N_i)) for normalization, content repr, ancestors, and sorting/serialization, besides stored nodes.

- `delete_path` traverses to the parent and detaches one subtree pointer, then recomputes ancestors. Explicit algorithm time: O(P + sum(c_i log c_i + N_i)). Extra space: O(P + d + max(c_i + N_i)). Python object reclamation adds O(q) work for q removed nodes, separate from the pointer-detach operation.
- `root_hash` is O(1) after updates maintain hashes.
solutionGuide: Represent directories and files as nodes. Recompute ancestors from the changed leaf back to the root so `root_hash()` stays constant time.
